common_name: Flamenco Samba Cuphea (Vivid Orange-Red Hummingbird Cuphea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Flamenco Samba blooms nonstop through summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, feeding regularly through the growing season to fuel its long bloom period. Flamenco Samba produces a dense cover of small, tubular, vivid orange-red flowers with a dark tip, held closely against fine-textured foliage on a mounding, well-branched plant that stays covered in bloom from late spring through frost without deadheading. Like other hummingbird cupheas, it draws hummingbirds reliably wherever it is planted, and its compact, self-cleaning habit makes it a low-maintenance choice for borders, containers, and mass plantings. Pinch or lightly shear leggy growth in midsummer to keep the plant dense, and protect from frost, since it is grown as a warm-season annual or tender perennial outside zone 9 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Imperial Blue's deeper blue flowers make it a strong choice for beds and large containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Imperial Blue is a Cape plumbago selection bred for consistently rich, deep cobalt-blue flowers, a noticeably more saturated color than the pale sky-blue of the straight species, held in loose clusters at the branch tips nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 9. Its sprawling, semi-vining shrub habit can be left loose and informal or trained against a fence or trellis for more height, and the flower color draws butterflies steadily through the warm season. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well once rooted in; cut back hard in late winter to remove any cold damage and encourage a fresh flush of dense, floriferous new growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Variegata is root-hardy in zone 9a with freeze protection, dying back in hard freezes but recovering from the roots in spring.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. Variegata carries the same arching, semi-weeping branches and clusters of small lavender-blue flowers followed by golden-yellow berries as the straight species, but each leaf is edged in a clean creamy-white margin, giving the shrub a brighter, more textured look even when not in bloom or fruit. The flowers and later the hanging clusters of golden berries both draw pollinators and birds, extending the plant's ornamental season well past the bloom period. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect dieback to the ground followed by vigorous spring resprouting from the roots; prune in late winter to shape and remove any cold-damaged wood.

common_name: Sheena's Gold Duranta (Bright Gold-Leaved Golden Dewdrop)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Place in full sun for the most intense golden foliage color; plants in shade develop a greenish tint.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil for the brightest foliage color. Sheena's Gold is a compact, golden-foliaged duranta similar in habit to Gold Mound but with a slightly more intense, brighter yellow leaf color that holds well through the heat of summer, brightening a mixed bed or hedge even between the light lavender-blue bloom flushes. Like other durantas, it is fast-growing and can be sheared to maintain a formal hedge shape or left looser as an informal flowering shrub, and it draws pollinators when in bloom. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect dieback to the ground followed by vigorous spring resprouting from the roots; prune in late winter to shape and remove cold-damaged wood.

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Tiny Mice blooms nonstop through summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, feeding regularly through the growing season to fuel its long bloom period. Tiny Mice earns its playful name from small, curled, deep red-purple flowers with two upright dark petals and a fuzzy white base that together resemble tiny mouse faces peeking out of the foliage, a whimsical variation on the standard bat-face cuphea flower shape found in other Cuphea llavea cultivars. Its dwarf, compact habit stays low and mounded, well suited to edging, small containers, and the front of a mixed border where larger cuphea would overwhelm the space. Pinch leggy growth to keep the plant dense, and protect from frost, since it is grown as a warm-season annual or tender perennial outside zone 9 and warmer.
